web_title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup
book_title: Chapter 8: Reading the Tape — Trend, Volume & Momentum Opportunity
title: A Bounce Into Supply
question: Is the chart showing a Weinstein Stage 2 advance with volume and relative-strength confirmation, or a retest inside a larger base or top?

epigraph.quote: It never was my thinking that made the big money for me. It always was my sitting.
epigraph.author: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923), the Livermore character on patience

web_blocks.html: Data basis. The verified session cutoff is Thursday 12 Nov 2026, the last Nifty 50 bar confirmed (25,299.35); the 13 Nov bar was not yet confirmed when the market-facts ledger was built [4]. Every close, average, RSI, ATR and volume figure that follows comes from that ledger (Yahoo daily bars) unless labelled 13 Nov TradingView print [40]. That print, pulled at 17:29 PST after the NSE close, shows ₹1,190.10 (+4.19% on the ₹1,142.20 ledger close), a high near ₹1,196.50 and volume of about 54,757, only 0.60x its 30-day average [10]. The gain came without volume expansion, and the close sits 0.47% (₹5.56) under the ₹1,195.66 30-week average (our calculation). We anchor levels to 12 Nov and test them against the print.

Short answer. This is not a Stage 2 advance. After a 50.3% fall in the closing price from ₹1,634.4 (17 Dec 2024) to ₹813.0 (13 Mar 2026), the share rebounded to ₹1,503.6 on 2 Jul 2026, gave back 35.9% to ₹963.6 on 2 Nov, and then rose 14.6% between 3 and 12 Nov after the Q2 FY27 results (our calculation) [4][3]. That is a retest of overhead supply on thin volume, against flat averages between ₹1,120 and ₹1,195: a base attempt, not a confirmed advance.

Screening labels. The compiler's tables carry two tool heuristics that are not our valuation. One is the screener label 'Reasonable / In-line'. The other is TradingView's 'Strong Buy (+0.54)' technical rating, a tally of moving-average and oscillator signals on the 13 November print. Both sit beside a 76.0x trailing P/E and neither says what the price pays for. Chapters 7 and 9 govern the decision.

web_blocks.title: Weinstein stage assessment: three systems, one honest call

web_blocks.html: Weinstein's framework has four stages: a flat Stage 1 base, a Stage 2 advance above a rising 30-week average, a Stage 3 top where the average flattens, and a Stage 4 decline below a falling average. His Stage 2 test is a decisive weekly close above the 30-week average on expanding volume [111]. Our feeds disagree, so we show all of them.

web_blocks.takeaway: No source calls this a Stage 2 advance; the only live disagreement is whether the chart is a top that has failed or a base that has not yet worked.

web_blocks.html: Our call follows the weekly average. The 30-week SMA peaked at ₹1,249.2 on 20 Jun 2025, fell to ₹1,002.8 by 15 May 2026, and has recovered to ₹1,193.0, up ₹190.2 in 26 weeks but down ₹1.1 over four (our calculation) [40]. The last weekly close above it was ₹1,197.1 on 25 Sep 2026; over 52 weeks the stock closed 26 weeks above and 26 below. That is base-building behaviour, and a base after a 50% drawdown must prove itself. Price has not closed decisively above the average on volume, so Stage 2 is unproven.

web_blocks.caption: Close ₹1,142.20 against its averages (12 Nov ledger; distances are our calculation)
web_blocks.takeaway: Five averages bunch between ₹1,109 and ₹1,193 around the price: a compression zone, not a trend, and only 15% of the last 60 sessions closed above the 50-day.

web_blocks.html: The one clear demand event is results day. On 4 Nov volume was 273,535 shares, 2.7x the prior 20-day average, and the close rose 10.7% from ₹996.6 to ₹1,103.3 [40]. Then volume faded to 55,579 on 6 Nov, 31,444 on 9 Nov, and 56,720 on 12 Nov, a +3.22% day at 0.49x the 20-day average of 114,224 (our calculation). The 50-session up/down volume ratio of 2.04 looks accumulation-tilted but is dominated by the 4 Nov spike, and the ledger counts 5 distribution days in 25 sessions [4].

web_blocks.caption: Shareholding pattern, selected quarters (blind snapshot from Screener; changes are our calculation)
web_blocks.takeaway: Domestic institutions added 0.95 pt in September while foreigners and promoters stood still: a modest, real signal that predates the results-day spike.

web_blocks.html: The 0.95 pt DII increase is roughly 2.23 lakh shares of 2.347 Cr (our calculation) [5]. It is a positive, but the quarter ended on 30 Sep, so it cannot explain the 4 Nov volume. Malabar India Fund Ltd held 26,60,000 shares (11.33%) per the annual report [2]; if it sits inside the 13.79% FII line, which the pack does not confirm, one holder is about 82% of foreign ownership (our calculation). No bulk-deal or block-deal data was retrieved for November, so we cannot say who bought on 4 Nov and will not infer it.

web_blocks.title: Relative strength, regime and the multi-timeframe lens

web_blocks.html: The market is healthy. The Nifty 50 is in an uptrend with narrow breadth: 76.8% of the breadth pool is above its 50-day, 4 distribution days are logged, and 9 of 11 sectors are above their 20-day and 50-day averages [4]. Xpro's relative strength against the Nifty is -2.11% over 63 sessions and -13.54% over 28. It is a laggard in a rising tape, and a laggard that bounces is not a leader resuming; the +14.11% two-week gain has only begun to repair that.

The shorter the timeframe, the better the picture. Weekly RSI is 52.09, neutral. Daily RSI is 63.39 on the 13 Nov print (59.71 on the ledger); TradingView's rating is +0.54. The 4-hour RSI is 67.69 with price above its 20-EMA (₹1,104.96) and 50-SMA (₹1,043.82): an intraday turn up and our best short-term evidence [10]. But the weekly chart decides the stage, and it has not turned.

As a base, the pattern is wide and loose, not a tight volatility-contraction setup. Bollinger bandwidth is 23.2% and ATR(14) is ₹53.17, 4.7% of price. The 63-session closing range of ₹963.6 to ₹1,389.7 is a 44.2% spread; weekly closes slid 26.9% from ₹1,325 to ₹968, then rebounded 18.0% (our calculation). A launch-ready base shows shrinking swings and dried-up volume at its lows; here swings remain large and volume has dried up only on the bounce.

web_blocks.caption: Resistance and support, distance from the 12 Nov close of ₹1,142.20 (our calculation)
rows: 63-session closing highs: first level that repairs the structure
30-week SMA (1,193.0 / 1,195.66) and 13 Nov intraday high near 1,196.50
web_blocks.takeaway: A floor near ₹1,105 sits 3% below and a ceiling at ₹1,195-1,200 sits 5% above: the stock is boxed in a narrow band inside a wide range.

web_blocks.title: Is there an actionable momentum edge now?

web_blocks.html: Not a clean one. The 4-hour turn is real, but the risk-reward is thin against nearby supply. An entry at ₹1,142.20 with a stop under ₹1,105 risks ₹37.2 (3.26% of the entry price) to make ₹53.5 (4.68%) at ₹1,195.7: 1.44:1, which needs a win rate near 41% to break even. The 4.5:1 ratio to ₹1,310 (+14.7%) exists only if ₹1,195 clears on volume, the missing ingredient. At the 13 Nov print, an entry of ₹1,190.10 with the same stop risks ₹85.1 (7.15% of the entry price) for 0.88:1 to ₹1,264.6 and 1.41:1 to ₹1,310 (our calculation). A stop only 0.7 ATR away sits inside one ordinary day's range: noise, not protection.

web_blocks.title: Both sides, and what flips or fails the structure

web_blocks.html: Technical bull case. The 4-hour chart has turned up, daily RSI is firm without being overbought, results-day demand was real, the up/down volume ratio is 2.04, the 200-day average is rising, and two-week relative strength has improved. Price sits within 0.5% of the 30-week average after a 23.5% rise from the 2 Nov low (our calculation).

Technical bear case. The stock lags the Nifty over 28 and 63 sessions, the 50-day is falling, and only 15% of the last 60 sessions closed above it. The rally rests on thin volume (0.49x on 12 Nov, 0.60x on 13 Nov), so overhead supply is untested. A 50.3% drawdown over 309 sessions shows the stock can lose half its value, and weekly RSI of 52 says the longer chart has not turned.

Flip and failure. The structure turns constructive on a weekly close above ₹1,200 on weekly volume of at least 1.5x the 20-day average week (about 8.6 lakh shares, which is 1.5 × 5 × the 20-day daily average of 114,224; our calculation), with ₹1,310-1,390 as the repair zone. It fails on a close back under ₹1,105-1,110, which reopens ₹963.6-940.1 and then the ₹913.8 and ₹817.8 pivots. Neither has occurred. The stock is not in NSE F&O, so no listed options exist to express a view [10].
Trigger: a weekly close above ₹1,200 on weekly volume of at least 1.5x the average week (about 8.6 lakh shares) makes the stock a Stage 2 candidate; a close under ₹1,105-1,110 cancels it.

book_paragraphs: A chart does not tell you what a business is worth, only what other people have been willing to pay and how eagerly. So this chapter has a narrow job: to ask whether the tape is giving us a good moment to act. First, the housekeeping. The verified session cutoff for this dossier is Thursday 12 Nov 2026, the last day the benchmark bar was confirmed, and the ledger closes the share at ₹1,142.20. By the time I am writing, a later 13 Nov print from TradingView shows ₹1,190.10, up 4.19%, on volume of only 0.60 times the 30-day average [10][4]. I keep the 12 Nov numbers as my anchor and treat the later print as a test of them.

Is this a fresh advance, or a stock catching its breath inside something bigger? My answer is the second. The share fell 50.3% from its closing high of ₹1,634.4 in December 2024 to ₹813.0 in March 2026. It rebounded to ₹1,503.6 in July, fell back to ₹963.6 on 2 Nov, and then jumped 14.6% to ₹1,142.20 after the Q2 results [4][3]. That is not a staircase. It is a roller coaster that is now parked under a ceiling of flat averages.

To read the ceiling, borrow a map from Stan Weinstein, who divided a stock's life into four stages [111]. In Stage 1 the stock goes sideways after a decline and the 30-week average, the simple average of thirty weekly closes, flattens. In Stage 2 the price climbs above a rising 30-week average on growing volume; that is where the big money is made. In Stage 3 the average flattens again and the price chops around it as the buyers tire. In Stage 4 the price slides under a falling average. A stage is a description of where you are in the story, not a prediction.

The data sources disagree about where Xpro sits, and I think you should see the disagreement rather than a tidy answer. Our market-facts ledger says Stage 3, a topping or pullback pattern. TradingView's stage tool says Stage 1, with the stock consolidating near the 30-week average at ₹1,195.66 and a support zone of ₹1,105.64 to ₹1,150.62. A separate TradingView text label says the trend is broken below both the 50-day and 200-day averages, but its own numbers put the price about 5% above the 50-day and 6% above the 200-day, so that label is out of date. TheWrap's Stage 2 dashboard, built on data to 8 Nov, does not list the stock at all among 465 names [112].

My own call is a late Stage 3 to 4 slide that has become a Stage 1 base attempt. The 30-week average peaked at ₹1,249.2 in June 2025, sank to ₹1,002.8 in May 2026, and has crept back to ₹1,193.0, flat over the last four weeks. Over the last 52 weeks the share closed 26 weeks above and 26 weeks below that line. The last weekly close above it was ₹1,197.1 on 25 Sep. That is a stock that has stopped falling, not yet a stock that has started rising.

Now the picture of the averages. The close of ₹1,142.20 is 0.8% above the 50-day (₹1,132.88, falling by about 3.5% in twenty sessions), 1.8% above the 200-day (₹1,121.65, rising slightly), 3.0% above the 10-week exponential average of ₹1,109.0 and almost exactly on the 40-week exponential average of ₹1,143.8. It is 4.3% below the 30-week average. When five averages bunch together within a few percent, the stock is not trending, it is deciding. Only 15% of the last 60 sessions closed above the 50-day average, so the decision has gone against the bulls more often than not.

What about volume, the footprint of institutions? On 4 Nov, results day, 273,535 shares changed hands, 2.7 times the prior 20-day average, and the share rose 10.7% in one session. That is a real burst of demand. But look at what followed: 55,579 shares on 6 Nov, then 31,444, and 56,720 on 12 Nov, when the share rose 3.22% on only 0.49 times its 20-day average. A rise on half the normal turnover does not suggest that buyers are lining up. The up-day to down-day volume ratio of 2.04 sounds friendly, but it is driven by that one spike, and the ledger counts five distribution days in the last 25 sessions [4].

The shareholding table adds a footnote, not a headline. Domestic institutions rose from 2.94% to 3.89% in the September quarter, a gain of 0.95 points or about 2.2 lakh shares by our arithmetic. Promoters held at 40.32% and foreign institutions edged from 13.81% to 13.79% [5]. The annual report lists Malabar India Fund Ltd at 11.33% [2]; if that fund is counted in the foreign line, about 82% of foreign ownership sits with one name. The quarter ended on 30 Sep, so none of this explains the November volume, and I retrieved no bulk-deal or block-deal data to tell you who bought on results day. I would rather say so than guess.

Relative strength is where the honesty gets uncomfortable. The Nifty 50 is in an uptrend, though with narrow breadth: 76.8% of its breadth pool is above the 50-day average and nine of eleven sectors are above their 20-day and 50-day averages [4]. Against that, Xpro trails the index by 2.11% over 63 sessions and 13.54% over 28 sessions. It is a laggard in a rising market. Even the last two weeks, when the share gained 14.11%, have only started to repair a gap.

Look at the shorter timeframes and the picture brightens. The weekly RSI, a 0 to 100 gauge of momentum, is 52, neutral. The daily reads 59.7 on the ledger and 63.4 on the later print, and the 4-hour chart reads 67.7 with the price above its 4-hour 20-period average of ₹1,104.96, an intraday turn up [10]. Bollinger bandwidth, a measure of how wide the price swings are against their norm, is 23.2%, and the daily range is 4.7% of the price. Good setups usually show swings narrowing and volume drying up at the lows, a pattern traders call volatility contraction. Here the swings are still wide: the 63-session closing range runs from ₹963.6 to ₹1,389.7, a 44.2% spread. Daily momentum turned up first, which is how recoveries start, but the weekly chart decides the stage, and it has not turned.

Where would the market argue the point? On the upside, the first ceiling is ₹1,195 to ₹1,200, where the 30-week average and the 13 Nov intraday high of about ₹1,196.50 meet. Above that sit the ₹1,264.6 pivot, the ₹1,310 to ₹1,389.7 zone of 63-session highs, the July high of ₹1,503.6 and the 52-week high of ₹1,574.8. Below, the floor is ₹1,105 to ₹1,110, where the 10-week and 4-hour averages cluster, then the 20-day average at ₹1,030, the November low of ₹963.6, the 20-day swing low of ₹940.1, the pivots at ₹913.8 and ₹817.8, and finally the March trough of ₹813.0. The stock is boxed between a floor 3% below and a ceiling 5% above.

Is there a trade in that box? Not a clean one, in my judgment. Suppose you bought at ₹1,142.20 and placed a stop just under ₹1,105. You would risk ₹37.2, or 3.26% of the entry price, to make ₹53.5 or 4.68% at the ceiling, a ratio of 1.44 to 1, which has to win about 41% of the time to break even. The 4.5 to 1 payoff to ₹1,310 exists only if the ₹1,195 ceiling gives way, and nothing about 0.6 times average volume says it will. Buy the 13 Nov print at ₹1,190.10 with the same stop and you risk ₹85.1, or 7.15% of the entry price, for 0.88 to 1 to the next pivot at ₹1,264.6. And a stop only 0.7 of an average daily range away is noise, not protection. Marks has a line I find useful here: 'You can't predict. You can prepare.' The preparation is to know your levels before the market tests them.

Let me give you the bull and the bear each in their best form. The bull says: the 4-hour chart turned, the daily momentum is healthy, results-day demand was real, the 200-day average is rising, and the stock sits within half a percent of the 30-week line after a 23.5% rise from the November low. The bear says: the stock trails the market, the 50-day is falling, volume faded to half of normal on the rally, overhead supply from 2025 is untested, the weekly chart is neutral, and this stock has already shown it can lose half its value. I find the bear's case stronger on evidence and the bull's case stronger on timing, which is why I would say 'wait for proof'.

What would settle it? A weekly close above ₹1,200 on weekly volume of at least 1.5 times the average week, about 8.6 lakh shares, would turn the structure into a genuine Stage 2 candidate, with ₹1,310 to ₹1,390 as the next repair zone. A close back under ₹1,105 to ₹1,110 would cancel the attempt and reopen ₹963.6 and ₹940.1. Graham's old line applies: 'In the short run, the market is a voting machine but in the long run it is a weighing machine.' On this chart the voting machine has begun to count again, but the votes are few. Even Chairman Sidharth Birla frames the business on a longer clock: 'Our approach is built for the long-term, where returns build as utilization ramps up over time' [88]. The tape, for now, is simply not on that clock. One last practical point: the stock is not in the NSE futures and options segment, so there is no listed options market to express a view, and any position is a plain equity exposure with the full drawdown history above.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A bounce is not a trend, and a chart cannot tell you how good the business is. This one tells us that the sellers of 2025 have not been cleared, that buyers appeared on results day but did not stay, and that the market has not yet voted for a new advance. Waiting for volume to confirm costs a few percent of upside. Buying before it does risks re-learning what a 50% drawdown feels like.
